title: What Building Relationships With Students Really Means ally-means/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin challenges the common assumption that building relationships with students means seeking out individual, personal conversations to get to know them better. He argues this approach is unrealistic for most classrooms and can actually backfire, making students—especially socially cautious ones—feel cornered, awkward, and wary of the teacher's motives. His alternative definition centers on influence rather than familiarity: relationships built through consistent trustworthiness (doing what you say) and consistent likability (being pleasant) develop naturally without deliberate one-on-one effort. He describes the resulting dynamic as effortless and organic, drawing in even quiet and shy students without the teacher needing to actively pursue them. The piece closes by reframing relationship-building as inseparable from good classroom management rather than a separate, additional task.
points: Seeking out individual students for personal conversations to build rapport is unrealistic and can backfire, making students uncomfortable.
Real influence, not familiarity, is the actual goal behind 'building relationships' with students.
Trustworthiness (doing what you say) and consistent likability naturally generate rapport without deliberate individual effort.
This organic approach draws in even quiet and shy students without the teacher needing to actively pursue them.
Building relationships isn't a separate task from classroom management—effective classroom management is itself the most reliable relationship-building strategy.
quotes: It’s common for teachers to misunderstand the term “building relationships.
You see, for most students, being cornered into a non-academic conversation with their teacher is uncomfortable—exceedingly so.
Although their heart is in the right place, what develops is a relationship of awkwardness and embarrassment.
But the goal of building relationships with students isn’t familiarity. It’s influence.
If your students trust you because you always do what you say will, and they like you because you’re consistently pleasant, then powerful, behavior-influencing rapport will happen naturally.
Even quiet and shy students—especially quiet and shy students—will come out of the woodwork to laugh and joke with you and exchange goofy smiles.
The fact is, the most effective way to build relationships with students also happens to be the most effective approach to classroom management.
